::: {#sol-nearest-image}

```{python}
#| code-fold: show
train_features = hand_features[train]
acc_nn_train = accuracy(
    labels[train][nearest(train_features, train_features)], labels[train]
)
acc_nn_test = accuracy(
    labels[train][nearest(hand_features[test], train_features)], labels[test]
)
print(round(acc_nn_train, 3), round(acc_nn_test, 3))
```

The rule gets `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * py$acc_nn_train)`% of the [training set](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/big-ideas.html#def-training-set) right,
but only `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * py$acc_nn_test)`% of the [test set](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/big-ideas.html#def-test-set),
worse than the `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * py$acc_mean_test)`% of the digit-average rule in @sol-held-out-averages.
On the training set, each image's nearest neighbor is usually itself,
so the rule mostly recalls labels it has already seen.
It falls short of 100% only where images of different digits
share both [feature](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/course-overview.html#def-feature) values.

This rule has learned the training images themselves rather than what the digits look like,
which lds calls [overfitting](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/big-ideas.html#def-overfitting).
Deep networks are flexible enough to memorize their training sets too,
even when the labels are assigned at random [@zhang2017rethinking],
so these notes judge every network on images it was not trained on.

:::
